passage:
Ramesh,
I'm writing this because when we talk, I lose my words.
On Saturday, when I said I wasn't ready to stay the night at your flat, you went quiet and then said, "If you really loved me, you wouldn't make me wait." I've heard some version of it three times now. Each time I feel guilty, then scared you'll leave, then angry that I feel scared.
So here it is, clearly. I do care about you. And I decide my own pace. Being ready is not a test of love. If you respect me, a "not yet" has to be okay without sulking or asking again the next day.
I told my friend Kokila about this yesterday. She asked whether I feel safe saying no to you. I want the answer to be yes. That part is up to you now.
Hansa

qa.q: What did Ramesh say on Saturday?
qa.a: "If you really loved me, you wouldn't make me wait."

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Hansa describe each time Ramesh says it?
qa.a: Hansa feels guilty, then scared that Ramesh will leave, then angry about feeling scared.

qa.q: What else, besides the letter, can help Hansa if the pressure continues?
qa.a: Keep talking with Kokila, the trusted friend who asked whether Hansa feels safe saying no, so Hansa isn't facing it alone.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Possibly defensive or embarrassed at first, but the letter gives Ramesh a clear choice: accept "not yet" or show that Hansa's pace isn't respected.

grounding: Shows a partner using love as pressure to go further, and the wise stance that one decides one's own pace and can lean on a trusted friend.

passage:
You asked why I've been so quiet, Rhea, so let me just say it. Parveen and I broke up on Sunday.
For weeks Parveen kept saying the same thing: "If you really loved me, you'd stop holding back." I almost gave in. Honestly, I almost did it just so I wouldn't lose Parveen. I'd lie awake thinking, is something wrong with me for not being ready?
On Sunday, in the park near college, I said it out loud: "I'm not ready, and I'm not going to be pushed." Parveen said, "Then this isn't love," and walked off.
And you know what, Rhea? I cried the whole auto ride home, but under the crying I felt light. Someone who respected me would have waited. I'm glad I didn't trade myself away to keep them.
So yes, this is me, Aparna, single and sad and weirdly proud. Now tell me about your week.

qa.q: When did Aparna and Parveen break up?
qa.a: On Sunday.

qa.q: What was Aparna afraid of while the pressure went on?
qa.a: Aparna was afraid of losing Parveen and anxious that something was wrong with not being ready, lying awake over it.

qa.q: What helped Aparna most, and what could help sooner if pressure like this returns?
qa.a: Saying clearly "I'm not ready, and I'm not going to be pushed"; talking to a trusted friend like Rhea early on would add support.

qa.q: How does Parveen seem to see Aparna's "not ready"?
qa.a: As proof of not being loved ("Then this isn't love"), treating Aparna's pace as a failure rather than a boundary.

grounding: Illustrates pressure framed as a test of love, the pull to give in from fear of loss, and choosing one's own pace.

passage:
At the Dussehra fair in Rampur, Farhan and Sharmila had slipped away from their friends to the quiet side of the ghat, behind the balloon sellers. They had been together four months. Sharmila leaned her head on his shoulder. "Nobody's around. We could go further down, near the boats."
Farhan's stomach tightened. Part of him wanted to just nod along and hope she'd read his silence. Instead he said, "Can I tell you something a bit awkward?"
"Always."
"I like this. Holding hands, sitting close. I'm not ready for more than that yet. I didn't want to say yes just to skip an uncomfortable moment."
Sharmila was quiet, then squeezed his hand. "I'm glad you told me instead of going along." She pointed at the giant wheel, lit up against the sky. "That, then?"
They walked back into the noise, fingers laced.

qa.q: How long had Farhan and Sharmila been together?
qa.a: Four months.

qa.q: What did Farhan feel when Sharmila suggested going near the boats?
qa.a: His stomach tightened; he felt uneasy and was tempted to nod along and hope she would read his silence.

qa.q: What did Farhan say, and why did it work?
qa.a: That he liked holding hands and sitting close but wasn't ready for more; saying it plainly let Sharmila respect it instead of guessing.

qa.q: How might Sharmila have seen the moment?
qa.a: Surprised for a second, then trusting and glad he was honest, which she shows by squeezing his hand and suggesting the giant wheel.

grounding: Illustrates being unsure about physical closeness and stating one's comfort plainly instead of hoping a partner will guess.

passage:
Outside Zainab's building in Koramangala, after their third dinner that month, Pankaj finally asked. "Could I come up tonight? Stay over?"
Zainab looked at her keys. "Not yet. I like you a lot. I'm just not there."
The words landed like a small slap. On the walk to the auto stand, a script ran in his head: send something short and cold, skip Friday's movie, let her feel it. His thumb was already on her chat.
He stopped under a streetlight. What exactly would that teach her? That telling him the truth costs something.
He typed instead: "Thanks for being honest with me. Friday still on?" Then he put the phone in his pocket without waiting.
By the time the auto reached Indiranagar, she had replied: "Friday's on. Thank you for hearing me." He still felt the sting. It was smaller than the relief.

qa.q: Where was Pankaj when he asked to come up?
qa.a: Outside Zainab's building in Koramangala.

qa.q: What did Pankaj feel after Zainab said "Not yet"?
qa.a: Hurt and stung, and briefly tempted to punish her with a cold message and by skipping Friday's movie.

qa.q: Why was Pankaj's final text a good choice?
qa.a: It thanked Zainab for her honesty and kept Friday's plan without bargaining, so telling the truth cost her nothing.

qa.q: How might Zainab see Pankaj's reply?
qa.a: As a sign that saying no is safe with him, which is why she thanks him for hearing her.

grounding: Shows being told not yet, feeling hurt, and choosing thanks and steadiness over sulking or coldness.

passage:
"So... Coorg, just us, next month?" Chandrika held up two bus tickets on her phone.
Ganga's smile faded a little. "Can I say not yet?"
"Not yet?"
"I'm not ready for an overnight trip, just the two of us. It's not about you."
Chandrika felt her face go hot. "But it's separate rooms, obviously, and we'd..." She stopped. "Sorry. I was about to bargain."
"You kind of were." Ganga laughed nervously.
"Okay. Thank you for telling me straight. I'll cancel the tickets."
"You're not upset?"
"A bit hurt, honestly. I'd built it up in my head. But I'd rather hear no than have you come along and feel trapped."
"Could we do a day trip instead? Nandi Hills, back by dinner?"
"I'll look up the morning bus." Chandrika put the phone away. "And I won't be weird at dinner about this. Promise."

qa.q: Where did Chandrika want to go next month?
qa.a: To Coorg, just the two of them.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika stop in the middle of her sentence about separate rooms?
qa.a: She felt hot-faced and hurt, noticed she was about to bargain, and caught herself out of respect for Ganga.

qa.q: What small steps showed Chandrika accepting the no?
qa.a: Thanking Ganga, cancelling the tickets, admitting the hurt honestly and promising not to be cold at dinner.

qa.q: How does Ganga respond once Chandrika stops bargaining?
qa.a: Ganga laughs nervously at first, then feels safe enough to offer a day trip to Nandi Hills instead.

grounding: Illustrates hearing not yet from a partner, feeling hurt, and stepping back with thanks instead of bargaining or sulking.

passage:
Yusuf, beta, you think those hostel boys are the first to tease someone? When I was nineteen, in the engineering hostel in Patiala, my wing called me "Baba-ji" because I'd never had a girlfriend. Every night: "Amandeep, still waiting for your rishta?"
So I did something foolish. I invented a girl in Chandigarh. Gave her a name, a college, even a fight we had. For a month they stopped teasing, and I felt sick every time someone asked about her. Then my roommate Gurmeet caught me when I mixed up her college. The teasing came back twice as hard, and now I was a liar too.
Only Gurmeet said, later, quietly, "Oye, you didn't need to make anyone up. Nobody's clock is the same." That stayed with me.
So I'm telling you this as your old Amandeep uncle: don't act out a story to fit in. Your pace is your own, and the ones who push you to prove it aren't your people.

qa.q: What nickname did the wing give Amandeep?
qa.a: "Baba-ji".

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel during the month of the invented girlfriend?
qa.a: He felt sick every time someone asked about her; the break from teasing came with guilt and a dread of being found out.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Amandeep's story, and what would have been a better choice before it?
qa.a: Being caught by Gurmeet; a better choice would have been to let the teasing pass and keep his own timeline instead of inventing a girl.

qa.q: How did Gurmeet see Amandeep's situation?
qa.a: With quiet kindness, seeing no need for him to prove anything because "nobody's clock is the same".

grounding: Shows being teased for inexperience, acting a part to fit in and regretting it, and a friend who does not need proof.

passage:
The bus back from Goa was two hours late, and nine tired students sat on their bags at the Mapusa stand, playing truth or dare to stay awake.
"Madhav, truth: ever kissed anyone?"
He could feel the grin waiting on Tushar's face. For a second he considered a made-up story about a girl from his coaching class. Instead he shrugged. "Nope."
"At twenty?" Tushar hooted. "Bro, we need to fix you. Party at the hostel tonight, I'll set you up."
Laughter. Madhav's ears burned. "No thanks. I'll get there when it's real."
"Boring!"
Then the rain started. Everyone crammed under the tin roof, and the game moved on. Arohi, squeezed beside him, said quietly, "For what it's worth, I haven't either. I just never say it out loud."
Madhav let out a breath he hadn't noticed holding. "Weird how that felt like the bravest thing I did all trip."

qa.q: How late was the bus back from Goa?
qa.a: Two hours late.

qa.q: What do Madhav's burning ears suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and exposed by the laughter, even though he chose to answer honestly.

qa.q: What would you advise Madhav if Tushar keeps pushing to set him up?
qa.a: Give the same calm no and spend more time with friends like Arohi who don't need him to prove anything.

qa.q: How does Arohi see Madhav's honest answer?
qa.a: As brave and familiar; it lets her quietly admit her own inexperience for the first time.

grounding: Illustrates being teased by friends for inexperience and keeping one's own timeline instead of acting to fit in.

passage:
Pankaj, before you go to that farewell party, let your Francis uncle tell you something from Goa, long ago. I was twenty, and I liked a girl called Lydia from my college. At a beach party we both drank too much feni. By midnight she could hardly stand, laughing, leaning on me, saying she wanted to go somewhere quiet.
One of my friends winked at me. And I'll be honest, for one moment my head was foggy too, and I thought, she's the one asking.
But she couldn't even say my name straight. That is not someone who can agree to anything. So I sat her down on a plastic chair, got her water, and found her roommate, Agnes. The two of us walked her home, and I slept on the porch outside till morning, just in case.
Next day Lydia thanked me, embarrassed. That friend who winked, I stopped drinking with him. So tonight, you keep an eye on your friends, and you all leave together.

qa.q: What did Francis give Lydia after sitting her down?
qa.a: Water.

qa.q: What was going on in Francis's mind when his friend winked?
qa.a: He felt tempted and foggy from the drink, briefly thinking "she's the one asking", before seeing that Lydia could not agree to anything.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why was the choice right?
qa.a: Noticing Lydia couldn't say his name straight; since she couldn't clearly agree, he got her water, found Agnes and walked her home safely.

qa.q: How might Lydia have felt the next day?
qa.a: Embarrassed but grateful and safe, knowing Francis protected her instead of taking advantage.

grounding: Shows judgement blurring at a party and the choice never to take advantage of someone impaired, but to get them home with friends.

passage:
The last metro from Saket left at 11:10, and it was 10:48 when Manoj found Ritika on the balcony of Yogesh's cousin's flat, giggling, her words sliding into each other.
"There you are," she said, catching his sleeve. "Let's find an empty room. Come on."
They'd been dating eight months. But tonight she was swaying, and her eyes weren't quite finding his.
"Not tonight," Manoj said gently. "You're really drunk, and I'm not doing anything you can't properly say yes to. Let's get you home."
She pouted, then sat down hard on a plant pot. He texted Yogesh: "Leaving now. Help?" Yogesh appeared with her bag and a bottle of water.
With twelve minutes left, they half-walked, half-carried her down three floors. On the metro she fell asleep on Manoj's shoulder. Yogesh stayed with them all the way to her PG, and Manoj waited until her roommate opened the door.

qa.q: When did the last metro from Saket leave?
Why did Manoj say "Not tonight" even though they had been dating eight months?
qa.a: He felt protective and cared about Ritika; since she was swaying and couldn't meet his eyes, he knew she could not properly agree.

qa.q: How did Manoj and Yogesh look out for Ritika?
qa.a: They brought her bag and water, got her to the metro together, rode all the way to her PG, and waited until her roommate opened the door.

qa.q: How might Ritika see the night once she is sober?
qa.a: Probably embarrassed but relieved and trusting, knowing Manoj refused to take advantage and made sure she got home safely.

grounding: Illustrates a partner who is impaired at a party and the wise choice to not assume agreement and to leave together with a friend.

passage:
Counsellor's note, hostel wellness room, Monday afternoon
Asif, second year, came in at 3 p.m., phone gripped in both hands. For three weeks he had been chatting with someone called Naveen whom he met in an online gaming group. Yesterday Naveen asked for private photos. Asif said no. Naveen replied, "Then I'll post our chats and tell everyone what you're like."
Asif kept saying, "I should never have talked to him so much." I told him clearly: refusing was right, the threat is Naveen's wrongdoing, not his fault, and there is nothing to feel guilty about.
With his permission we took screenshots together, and he blocked the account in front of me. I called the warden in, and we filed an online cyber crime complaint before 5 p.m. The warden will check on him tonight at dinner. We meet again on Wednesday.

qa.q: How long had Asif been chatting with Naveen?
qa.a: For three weeks.

qa.q: What does Asif's repeated "I should never have talked to him so much" suggest?
qa.a: He feels guilty and frightened, wrongly blaming himself for Naveen's threat.

qa.q: What was done that same afternoon to protect Asif?
qa.a: The counsellor told him refusing was right and not his fault, helped save screenshots, watched him block the account, brought in the warden and filed a cyber crime complaint before 5 p.m.

qa.q: What would have changed if Asif had sent the photos to stop the threat?
qa.a: He would have lost control of them for good, and the threats would likely have grown rather than stopped.

grounding: Shows being asked for private photos, refusing without guilt, and telling an adult and reporting when a threat follows.

passage:
Thursday night
Sachin asked again tonight. Photos, "just for me, you know I'd never show anyone." Third time this month.
I stared at the message for ten minutes. The old me would have felt guilty, like I was being a boring girlfriend. He even wrote, "Don't you trust me?"
But here's what I kept thinking: once a picture leaves my phone, it isn't mine anymore. Not his promise, not my trust, nothing can pull it back. Phones get lost. People break up. Chats get forwarded.
So I wrote: "I do trust you. My answer is still no, and it'll stay no. Please stop asking." Then I made instant noodles with my roommate and didn't check my phone for an hour.
He replied "ok fine" with nothing else. Whatever. If he asks again, I'm telling Didi.
— Pooja

qa.q: How many times had Sachin asked this month?
qa.a: Three times; tonight was the third time this month.

qa.q: What did Pooja feel when Sachin wrote "Don't you trust me?"
qa.a: A pull of guilt, the old fear of being a boring girlfriend, which she pushed past to stay firm.

qa.q: What makes Pooja's reply strong?
qa.a: It separates trust from the request, gives a no that will stay no, asks him to stop, and she plans to tell Didi if he keeps asking.

qa.q: How might Sachin see the "ok fine" moment?
qa.a: Possibly disappointed or sulky, but her clear answer leaves him knowing it won't change.

grounding: Illustrates being asked for private photos, knowing control is lost once sent, and refusing without guilt.

passage:
Rain hammered the windows of the 9:40 bus to Kothrud, and every seat was full. Avni stood holding the rail when the man behind her pressed closer than the crowd required.
She shifted. He shifted too.
"Move back," she said, loud enough for the nearby row to hear. "Right now."
He smirked. "Bus is crowded, madam."
"Then stand somewhere else." Her voice shook, but she didn't lower it. She squeezed forward to the conductor. "That man in the grey jacket keeps pushing against me."
The conductor turned. "You. Get down at the next stop." Two women nodded at Avni.
Her phone was at four percent. She called Vasudha, her hostel roommate. "I'm okay. Meet me at the stop?"
Vasudha was waiting under an umbrella. That night, together, they wrote to the women's helpline and the warden with the bus number and time. "It's not on you," Vasudha said. "Not one bit."

qa.q: Which bus was Avni on?
qa.a: The 9:40 bus to Kothrud.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling when she said "Move back"?
qa.a: Scared and angry, since her voice shook, but determined not to lower it.

qa.q: Which of Avni's steps kept her safer?
qa.a: A firm, loud no, moving next to the conductor and reporting the man, calling Vasudha, and writing to the helpline and warden with the bus number and time.

qa.q: How does Vasudha see what happened?
qa.a: As entirely the man's doing, not Avni's fault, so she waits with an umbrella and helps report it.

grounding: Shows unwanted advances from a stranger on a bus and the response of a firm no, moving away, reporting, and being told it is not her fault.

passage:
For two weeks, a man from the third floor of Rafiq's paying-guest building in Hyderabad had been finding reasons to talk to him: at the water cooler, on the stairs, outside the bathroom. Then the messages started. "You look good today." "Come to my room, we'll chill." Rafiq replied once: "Not interested. Please stop." The next morning there was a note under his door.
Rafiq told no one at first. It felt ridiculous, a grown guy scared to walk down a corridor. He started showering at odd hours to avoid it.
On Friday, Sharmila, who managed the building, noticed him taking the long staircase again. "Everything okay, Rafiq?"
He showed her the messages and the note. She read them slowly, then looked up. "Thank you for telling me. This isn't your fault. Save everything and block him now. I'm speaking to him today, and if it continues, he leaves."
By evening, the man's number was blocked and he had a written warning from the management.

qa.q: Where did the man find reasons to talk to Rafiq?
qa.a: At the water cooler, on the stairs and outside the bathroom.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq start showering at odd hours?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and embarrassed, so he tried to avoid the man instead of telling anyone.

qa.q: What did Sharmila do that helped?
qa.a: She thanked Rafiq, said it wasn't his fault, told him to save everything and block the man, spoke to the man that day and gave a written warning.

qa.q: How does Sharmila see Rafiq's report?
qa.a: As a serious problem in her building, not something ridiculous, and she acts on it the same day.

grounding: Illustrates unwanted advances from a stranger in a hostel-like building, a firm no, and reporting to the person in charge; it is not the target's fault.

passage:
The power had gone out in the girls' hostel, and Damini was revising by phone torch for the next morning's internal exam when Jahnavi sat on the edge of her bed and didn't open a book.
"Something happened at Karan's birthday," Jahnavi said finally. "I said no. He didn't stop."
Damini put the phone down, torch facing the ceiling. A question rose in her about why Jahnavi had gone to his room, and she swallowed it. "I believe you. It's not your fault. Thank you for telling me."
Jahnavi was shaking. "Please don't tell the others. People will talk."
"I won't tell anyone for gossip. But you shouldn't carry this alone. Can we go to Dr. Menon, the hostel counsellor, right now? I'll stay with you."
Twenty minutes later, exam forgotten, they were in the counsellor's room. Dr. Menon listened, told Jahnavi again that she was not to blame, and that same night called the campus committee and a support helpline with her, explaining every choice Jahnavi still had.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi say happened at Karan's birthday?
qa.a: "I said no. He didn't stop."

qa.q: What thought did Damini swallow, and what was she feeling?
qa.a: A doubting question about why Jahnavi went to his room; Damini felt shaken but chose belief over blame, so Jahnavi felt safe to keep talking.

qa.q: How did Damini help Jahnavi find safe support?
qa.a: She believed her, promised no gossip, and took her to the hostel counsellor that same night, staying beside her.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi feel when Damini says "I believe you"?
qa.a: Less alone and less ashamed; being believed first made it possible to go to the counsellor.

Ujjwal had cancelled plans three times, so when he finally met Ayesha at the café near the Anna Nagar tower park, she noticed at once: sleeves pulled over his hands, cold coffee untouched.
"I don't know how to say this," he said. "At the internship party, a senior... I kept saying no. It didn't matter." He looked at the table. "Guys aren't supposed to... people will laugh."
Ayesha felt her stomach drop, but kept her voice steady. "I'm not laughing. I believe you. It's not your fault, and it isn't smaller because you're a man."

"Your name isn't what matters right now. You are. Would you talk to someone trained? I'll sit with you."

qa.a: It eases his fear of mockery and shame, making it possible for him to nod and reach out for help.

passage:
Sarita,
You told me on Tuesday that at Meghna's party I kept pulling you onto my lap even after you moved away twice, and that you felt embarrassed and uncomfortable in front of everyone.
My first reaction, I'm ashamed to say, was to argue. I said I was only being affectionate, that you were overreacting. I spent that night building a case in my head about my intentions.
Then I read your message again. You didn't say I meant harm. You said you moved away twice and I didn't notice. That's true. I was paying attention to what I wanted, not to you.
I'm sorry. Not "sorry if you felt", just sorry that I did it. From now on, if you move away, I stop. I won't touch you in public unless we've both made clear it's okay. And if I get it wrong again, I want you to feel safe telling me.
Irfan

passage:
You want to know why Indu and I weren't talking last week, Farah? Okay. It was me.
We were at her sister's place, and I kept sneaking up and hugging her from behind while she cooked. She said "stop" once, laughing, so I didn't. Then she put the ladle down and said, not laughing, "You made me really uncomfortable. I said stop."
And my first reaction? "I was just being cute! You're making it sound like something awful." I actually said that. Then I sulked for two days.
On the third day I asked her to explain, and I just listened. She said the laugh was her being polite, and that "stop" means stop even if she smiles. I didn't argue. I said sorry, properly, no "but".
So yes, it's me, Ankita, telling you I got it wrong. Now I ask before I hug her from behind, and I don't treat a laugh as a yes.

passage:
Dear Kunal,
I've tried to say this over coffee twice and ended up talking about the weather, so here it is on paper. It feels less embarrassing this way.
We've been together three months, and I realise I've been hoping you'd just guess what I want. That's not fair to either of us.
So: I want us to be exclusive. I like holding hands in public, but I'm not comfortable kissing in front of friends. And about going further physically, I want to go slowly, and I want us to talk about it, not drift into it.
I'd really like to hear what you want too, even if it's different. Different doesn't scare me. Silence does.
Can we talk on Saturday, at the lake, no phones? You can laugh at how formal this letter is. I'm laughing a bit too.
Ganga

qa.q: How long have Ganga and Kunal been together?
qa.a: Three months.

qa.q: Why did Ganga choose to write instead of talking over coffee?
qa.a: Ganga felt too embarrassed to say it aloud, having twice ended up talking about the weather instead.

qa.q: What makes Ganga's letter a respectful way to discuss expectations?
qa.a: It says plainly what Ganga wants and doesn't want, invites Kunal's view even if it differs, and proposes a calm talk at the lake.

qa.q: What would change if Ganga had kept hoping Kunal would guess?
qa.a: Kunal might misread signals, and both could end up hurt or uncomfortable without knowing why.

grounding: Shows discussing what each partner wants plainly and respectfully instead of expecting them to read your mind.

passage:
Lakshmi, you asked how Arvind and I stopped fighting every weekend. Honestly? I stopped expecting him to read my mind.
For months I'd sulk when he booked a movie instead of a quiet dinner, or when he held my hand at my cousin's wedding while I didn't want the whole family watching. I thought, if he really knew me, he'd know.
Then one night, at the dhaba near the highway, I just said it: "Can we each say what we want, even the embarrassing stuff?" My face was burning. I told him I want slow, private affection, and a clear talk before we go further. He said he wants us to be more open in public and to start planning a future together. We don't want the same things on everything.
But now we know. We agreed on some, and we're still talking about the rest.
So that's me, Sangeeta, queen of silent sulking, reformed. Mostly.

qa.q: Where did Sangeeta start the honest talk?
qa.a: At the dhaba near the highway.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling when asking "Can we each say what we want"?
qa.a: Embarrassed, with a burning face, but hopeful and determined to stop the silent sulking.

qa.q: What went wrong before, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Sangeeta expected Arvind to guess and sulked when he didn't; saying plainly what each wanted let them agree on some things and keep talking about the rest.

qa.q: How might Arvind see the conversation at the dhaba?
qa.a: As a relief: he finally learns what Sangeeta wants and can share his own wishes openly.

grounding: Illustrates talking about expectations in a relationship without embarrassment, accepting differences instead of expecting mind-reading.
